blocks.text: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Methane (CH₄) is the simplest member of this family. The homologous series of alkanes with condensed structural formulae and molecular formulae are shown in Table 11.1.

blocks.title: Did You Know?
blocks.text: Butane is a fuel used in lighters. Isobutane is used as a propellant in products such as shaving gel.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Table 11.1 heptane is printed as C₇H₁₀ with the condensed structure CH₃ CH₂ CH₃ CH₂ CH₂ CH₂ CH₃. By CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ heptane is C₇H₁₆, CH₃ CH₂ CH₂ CH₂ CH₂ CH₂ CH₃ (five CH₂ groups between the two CH₃ ends). ‘Butana’ is butane.

What we obtain after the removal of one hydrogen atom from an alkane is called an alkyl group. The resulting alkyl groups are named by replacing –ane of the alkanes with –yl. Few examples are shown in Table 11.2 & Table 11.3.

blocks.text: For alkanes with more than two carbon atoms, more than one alkyl groups can be derived.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Table 11.3 butane is printed as H₃CH₀CH₂CH₃; butane is H₃CCH₂CH₂CH₃. The IUPAC name of the tert-butyl group (CH₃)₃C– is 1,1-dimethylethyl, not ‘1,1-Dimethylpropyl’: its longest chain from the attached carbon has two carbons. ‘iso-Propul’ and ‘Iso-Butyle’ are isopropyl and isobutyl.
